CARBON

Carbon Content

  • In earth's crust: 0.025%.
  • In atmosphere: 0.03%.

Basic Features of Carbon

CatenationTetravalency
Unique ability to form long chains of C-C bondCapability to form 4 bonds with other atom of carbon or other monovalent elements
No other element exhibit catenation property as much as CarbonCarbon forms a strong and stable bond due to its small size

Carbon's Ability to Catenate

  • The electronic configuration of carbon plays a key role in its ability to exhibit catenation. Carbon has a total of 6 electrons, with 2 in inner shell and 4 in the outer shell. Its small atomic size allows it to form stronger C-C bonds compared to other elements, making carbon the most effective element in catenation.

Bonding of Carbon with Oxygen

[Diagram: O=C=O → CO₂]

  • Oxygen has 6 e⁻ and requires 2 more electrons to complete its Octet. Carbon requires 4 more e⁻ to complete its octet.

Bonding of Carbon with Hydrogen

  • Carbon and hydrogen form a covalent bond (specifically, a nonpolar covalent bond) by sharing electrons, where carbon shares its outer valence electrons with up to four hydrogens to complete their outer shells and this allows both carbon and hydrogen to achieve stable electronic configurations.

Covalent Bond

A covalent bond is a chemical bond that involves the sharing of electrons to form electron pairs between atoms. Covalent compounds exhibit weak boiling and melting point because the intermolecular forces between their molecules are weak. Covalent bonds are usually formed between non-metals.

Oxygen

  • Oxygen cannot form long chains of bonding like carbon because of its small size and high electronegativity, and because it lacks d-orbitals.

Allotropes of Carbon

Allotropy

  • Allotropy is the property of some chemical elements to exist in two or more different forms, in the same physical state, known as allotropes of the elements.
  • Allotropes of carbon are: Diamond, graphite, fullerenes, graphene, etc.

Diamond

  • It has a 3D-tetrahedral structure with sp³ hybridisation.
  • Diamond is a bad conductor of electricity.
  • In the structure of diamond, each carbon atom is bonded to 4 other carbon atoms.
  • It can be synthesized by subjecting pure carbon to very high temperature and pressure.
  • Diamond is the hardest naturally occurring substance.
  • Diamond and crystalline silicon is isomorphous.
  • It has the highest refractive index (2.42).

Uses of Diamond

  • It is used for cutting glasses.
  • It is used for sharpening hard tools.
  • It is used for manufacturing Tungsten (W) filament.
Isomorphous: It means having similar shapes or crystalline structures.
Diamond is covalent, yet it has high melting point because it has 3D network involving strong C-C Bonds that are difficult to break.

Graphite

  • It has a 2-D layered structure (held by Van der Wall forces) and sp² hybridisation.
  • It features carbon arranged in hexagonal plane array.
  • Each carbon is bonded to three other carbon atoms, forming a hexagonal lattice. The fourth electron remains delocalized, contributing to electron conductivity.
  • Graphite is a good conductor of heat and electricity.
  • It is the most stable form of carbon.
Graphite is soft and slippery because it has a layered structure weakly bonded together because of which they could slide over each other and that is why mostly used in lubricants.

Uses of Graphite

  • Graphite is used in making electrodes.
  • It is used in pencil lead.
  • It is used as a dry lubricant.
  • It is used as a moderator for fast moving neutron in atomic reactors.

Fullerenes

  • It is also known as Buckminsterfullerene (C60).
  • It is known for its hollow, cage-like structures arranged in patterns of 20 hexagonal rings and 12 pentagonal rings.
  • A hexagonal ring can be fused with hexagonal or pentagonal ring, but a pentagonal ring can only be fused with hexagonal ring.
  • It has sp² hybridisation.
  • It contains both single and double bond with other 3 carbon atoms.
  • Fullerenes is the purest form of carbon.

Graphene

  • Graphene is a single-atom-thick layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, making it the thinnest material known. It exhibits exceptional electrical and thermal conductivity, making it an outstanding material for various technological applications.

  • Bond-line structure of propane

International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC)

  • It is a scientific organization that is responsible for naming hydrocarbons.
  • It publishes several books often referred to as "IUPAC Color Books".
  • Blue Book: Nomenclature of organic compounds.
  • Red Book: Nomenclature of inorganic compounds.

Examples:

  • CH₃-C≡C-CH₂-CH₃ (positions 1,2,3,4,5) → Pent-2-yne (Nearest position for double/triple/functional group)
  • CH₃-CH₂-CH₂-C≡CH → Pentyne
  • CH₃-CH₂-CH₂-CH₃ (positions 1,2,3,4) → 2-Methyl Butane (Look for continuous longest chain, CH₃ → Alkyl group)
  • CH₃ → Methyl
  • CH₃-CH₂ → Ethyl
  • CH₃-CH₂-CH₂ → Propyl
Root: It is the longest continuous chain of a compound.

HYDROCARBONS

Types of Hydrocarbons

Unsaturated HydrocarbonsSaturated Hydrocarbons
More than 1 bond between carbon atomsSingle bond between carbon atoms
Burns with yellow sooty flameGives clean blue flame however in limited supply of air gives sooty flame
  • Alkenes/Olefins — E.g. Ethene (Double bonds)
  • Alkynes — E.g. Ethyne/Acetylene (Triple bonds)
  • Alkanes/Paraffins — E.g. Ethane (Single bond)
  • Other examples: Benzene, anthracene, camphor
  • Other examples: Hexane, alcohol, butane
  • Alkanes → ane (General Formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — Butane)
  • Alkene → ene (General Formula: CₙH₂ₙ — Ethene)
  • Alkyne → yne (General Formula: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ — Propyne)
  • Ethene plays an important role in fruit ripening.
  • LPG gas contains butane and propane.
  • Acetylene is used for welding of metals.

Examples:

  • CH₃-CH₂-CH(CH₃)-CH₂-CH₃ → 3-Methyl Pentane
  • CH₃-CH₂-CH(CH₃)-C≡CH → 3-Methyl Pentyne

Homologous Series

  • It consist of one functional group, which decides the property of carbon compounds, regardless of length of carbon chain.
  • Homologous series differs by -CH₂ unit and mass by 14 units.
  • Chemical properties of homologous series remains same.
  • As the molecular mass increases, the melting point and boiling point also increases.

Homologous Series

AlkanesAlkynesAlcohols
CH₄C₂H₂CH₃OH
C₂H₆ (+CH₂)C₃H₄ (+CH₂)C₂H₅OH (+CH₂)
C₃H₈ (+CH₂)C₄H₆ (+CH₂)C₃H₇OH (+CH₂)
C₄H₁₀ (+CH₂)C₅H₈ (+CH₂)C₄H₉OH/CH₂ (+CH₂)

Isomers

  • Isomers are chemical compounds that have identical chemical formula but differ in properties and the arrangement of atoms in the molecule.
  • CH₃-CH₂-CH₂-CH₃ → C₄H₁₀ → Butane
  • CH₃-CH₂-CH(CH₃)-CH₃ → C₆H₁₄ → 3-Methyl Pentane

TRICK for Identifying No. of Isomers: 2^(n-4) + 1

Isomers In

  • Hexane: 2^(6-4) + 1 = 2² + 1 = 5
  • Heptane: 2^(7-4) + 1 = 2³ + 1 = 9
  • Octane: 2^(8-4) + 1 = 2⁴ + 1 = 16 + 1 + 1 = 18
  • Nonane: 2^(9-4) + 1 = 2⁵ + 1 = 32 + 1 + 2 = 35
  • Single bond: made of one σ bond
  • Double bond: made of one σ and one π bond
  • Triple bond: made of one σ and two π bond

Organic Compounds

Aliphatic/Acyclic Compounds

  • They are not aromatic (lack ring structure). E.g. Alkane, Alkene, Alkyne (open chain compounds).
  • Examples: Methane, Propane

Cyclic Compounds

  • They are compounds that form a ring structure. E.g. Benzene, Naphthalene.

Cyclical Formula

  • Alkane: CₙH₂ₙ
  • Alkene: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂
  • Alkyne: CₙH₂ₙ₋₄

Heterocyclic Compounds

  • They are cycling compounds that have atoms of at least two different elements in their ring structure.

Important heterocycles: Furan, Thiophene, Pyrrole, Pyridine, Pyrimidine, Imidazole, Oxadiazole, Isoxazole, Oxazole, Pyrazole, Isothiazole, Thiazole, Pyrazine, Isoquinoline, Quinoline, Benzofuran, Benzimidazole

Aromatic Compounds

  • They are group of compounds that have a cyclic conjugated structure and contain (4n+2) π electrons, making them particularly stable (Erich Huckel's Rule).
  • Examples: Benzene (Simplest aromatic compound), Toluene (Benzenoid aromatic compound)

Number of Covalent Compounds

  • CH₃-CH₂-CH₃ → 10 bonds
  • CH₃-CH(CH₃)-CH₃ → 13 bonds
  • Benzene structure → 15 bonds
  • Cyclohexane structure → 18 bonds

Chemical Properties of Carbon Compounds

  1. 1. Combustion: Carbon in all its allotropic form burns in Oxygen to give Carbon Dioxide along with the release of Heat + Light.

CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + Heat + Light (Combustion: flame)

  1. 2. Oxidation of Alcohol to Ethanoic Acid

CH₃-CH₂-OH → (H⁺/KMnO₄ OR H⁺/K₂Cr₂O₇) → CH₃-CO-OH (Ethanoic acid)

  • KMnO₄: Potassium permanganate
  • K₂Cr₂O₇: Potassium dichromate

This reaction is carried out in presence of oxidising agent

  1. 3. Addition Reaction: Unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen in presence of Catalyst (Ni, Pd) to give saturated hydrocarbons.

R₂C=CR₂ + H₂ (Ni/Pd) → R₂HC-CHR₂

  1. 4. Substitution Reaction: A hydrogen atom in a saturated hydrocarbon is replaced by a chlorine atom, forming a chlorinated derivative and hydrogen chloride, often in the presence of sunlight.

CH₄ + Cl₂ (Sunlight) → CH₃Cl + HCl (Methane → Chloromethane)

CH₃Cl + Cl₂ (Sunlight) → CH₂Cl₂ + HCl

CH₂Cl₂ + Cl₂ (Sunlight) → CHCl₃ + HCl (Chloroform)

CHCl₃ + Cl₂ (Sunlight) → CCl₄ + HCl

Vegetable Oil Vs Animal Fats

Vegetable OilAnimal Fats
Long unsaturated carbon chainsSaturated fats
Preferred for cookingHarmful for health

Boiling Point and Solubility of Hydrocarbons

  • Alkynes generally have slightly higher boiling point than alkenes and alkanes (Alkyne > Alkene > Alkane) because of the stronger intermolecular forces arising from the triple bond.

CH₃-CH₃ < CH₃-CH₂-CH₃ < CH₃-CH₂-CH₂-CH₃ (Ethane < Propane < Butane)

  • Alkenes have stronger intermolecular forces than alkanes due to the double bond, so their boiling point is higher than that of alkanes, but lower than alkynes.
  • As the number of carbon in alkane increases, its boiling point increases significantly. Also, molecule with strong intermolecular forces will have high boiling points.

Solubility of Hydrocarbons

  • Solubility decreases as the length of hydrocarbon chain increases.

C₂H₆ > C₃H₈ > C₄H₁₀

Important Carbon Compounds

  1. 1. Methanol
  • Methanol also known as Methyl alcohol is also called "wood spirit" because it was obtained in the initial stage by the destructive distillation of wood.
  • Intake of methanol in very small quantities can cause death. Methanol oxidises to methanal in liver and coagulates protoplasm.
  • Methanol also affects optic nerves, causing blindness.
  1. 2. Ethanol
  • It is a pleasant smelling carbon compound.
  • It is an active ingredients in alcoholic drinks.
  • Denatured spirit or alcohol is ethanol which is made unfit for drinking by adding poisonous substances like methanol that imparts a bad taste, foul smell, or colour. A blue dye is also added to it, so that it is easily recognized.
  • It is soluble in water in all proportion.
  • It is a good solvent and is used in medicines such as:
  1. 1. Tincture of iodine
  2. 2. Cough syrups

Reactions of Ethanol

  1. 1. Reaction with Sodium → Evolution of Hydrogen gas.

C₂H₅OH + Na → C₂H₅ONa + H₂ (g) (Ethanol)

  1. 2. Dehydration of Ethanol
  • On heating ethanol at 443K with excess Conc. Sulphuric acid (Dehydrating agent), it results in dehydration of ethanol to ethene.

C₂H₅OH (Conc. H₂SO₄) → CH₂=CH₂ (Ethanol → Ethene)

Alkyl group is also represented as -R

Different Types of Alcohol

  • Primary
  • Secondary
  • Tertiary
  1. 3. Ethanoic Acid (Acetic acid)
  • A 5-8% solution of acetic acid in water is called vinegar and is used widely as a preservative in pickles.
  • The melting point of pure ethanoic acid is 290K and hence it often freezes during winters and is called glacial acetic acid.
  1. 1. Reaction with Base
  • When ethanoic acid reacts with a base, it undergoes a neutralization reaction, forming a salt (an ethanoate) and water.

CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O (Ethanoic acid + Sodium hydroxide → Ethanoate)

  1. 2. Esterification Reactions
  • In an esterification reaction, a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, typically in the presence of an acid catalyst, to form an ester and water.

CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → CH₃CO-O-C₂H₅ + H₂O (Carboxylic acid + Removal of water → Ester + Water) (-oic group)

Ester

  1. 1. It is formed by reaction of acid and alcohol.
  2. 2. It is a sweet smelling substance used in making perfumes and flavouring agents.

Soap and Detergents

Saponification Reaction

  • This reaction is used in preparation of soaps. In this reaction, an ester is treated with a base (like sodium hydroxide) that breaks it down into an alcohol and a sodium salt of a carboxylic acid.
  • The ester is converted back to alcohol and sodium salt of carboxylic acid.

CH₃COOC₂H₅ (NaOH) → CH₃COONa + C₂H₅OH

  • Soaps are cleansing agents that are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids (also known as fatty acids).
  • Soap obtained remains in colloidal form and is precipitated from solution by adding NaCl.
  • The solution left after removing the soap contains glycerol which is later recovered by fractional distillation.

[Diagram: Micelle structure showing dirt trapped inside micelle with oil-soluble tail and water-soluble head]

Soap does not work in

  • Hard water: Because in hard water it reacts to form Calcium & Magnesium salts, which is an insoluble substance called Scum.
  • Acidic condition: Because it forms insoluble long chain fatty acids.
Cleansing action of soap is due to formation of micelles. It forms an emulsion in water and does not come together to precipitate because of ion-ion repulsion. Soap micelle shows Tyndall Effect, thus soap solution appears cloudy.

Detergents

  • Detergents are sodium salt of sulphonic acids or ammonium salts with Chloride, Bromide ions etc.
  • Detergents work in both hard and soft water.
  • They dissolve in water faster than soap.
Sodium benzoate is used as preservative in many foods, medicine, and cosmetics.
Friedrich Wohler in 1828 synthesised Urea (NH₂CONH₂) an Organic Compound from an Inorganic Compound named Ammonium Cyanate (NH₄CNO).
